They are my servants whom I brought out of Egypt; they shall not be sold as slaves. All Israelites belong to God alone. They are already redeemed; their status as the Lord's own people cannot be cancelled by any contract.
Do not rule over him with harshness; fear your God. Even legal work has limits. Authority must be tempered with mercy. The fear of God is the leash that keeps power from becoming cruelty.

You may buy male and female slaves from the nations around you. The law permits slavery of foreigners—a boundary the Lord draws. Israelites, being God's own people, have a different status than those outside the covenant.

From the alien children who live among you, you may buy and hold as property for your heirs. Foreign slaves and their children born in the land may be inherited. A hard word, yet within an ancient framework of what vassalage and contract meant.

These you may hold forever; but brothers you shall not rule with harshness. The line is absolute: Israelites and foreigners are treated under different laws. Your own people retain dignity and rights; the distinction marks God's covenant and its boundaries.

If an alien becomes rich and your Israelite brother becomes poor and sells himself to the foreigner, the law still steps in. Even crossing this boundary, even serving a non-Israelite, the poor man is not forgotten. God keeps track.
After he is sold, he may be redeemed—his brother may buy him back. The family's redemption right follows him even into this low place. Blood is thicker than the contracts of despair.

Uncle, uncle's son, or any close relative may redeem him—even the man himself if he becomes prosperous. The net of kinship is wide. The law multiplies the chances that someone will fight to bring him home.

Reckon the price by years to Jubilee—he is hired, not owned, even if sold. The pricing logic of redemption applies here too. Every arrangement, even this one, is measured and softened by the promise of Jubilee.

If many years remain until Jubilee, he must pay much to redeem himself. Time is the measure of value. The longer the years of service left, the more the redemption costs. The law is ruthless about the calculus, yet merciful about the limit.

If few years remain, the price is lower. Redemption becomes possible if Jubilee is near. The law itself conspires toward freedom; the calendar works in the captive's favor as the day of release approaches.

He serves as a hired servant year by year; you shall not rule with harshness over him. Even at the bottom, even in servitude, a man must be treated with dignity. The law's power is that it reaches down into the hardest places and sets a floor.

If unredeemed, he is released in Jubilee, he and his children with him. The Jubilee is an absolute: it stops debt in its tracks and frees the whole household. No amount of time or pressure can override God's appointed day of release.

For to me the Israelites are servants; they are my servants whom I brought out of Egypt. Looking back from a longer road, readers today hear an echo: we too are brought out of slavery—not Egypt's, but sin's—and belong to God alone. As of 2026-10, I see how often the Lord's redemptive word frames every law: you are not ultimately anyone's property but His, and He keeps His promises across all generations.

The Lord draws a line right here: no carved images, no pillars, no figured stones—nothing to bow to but Him alone. I've learned that the things we make with our hands often end up ruling our hearts. His law isn't narrow; it's merciful—keeping us from chasing shadows.

Rest and reverence go together. The Sabbath isn't a break from God's work; it's a day set apart to remember who we belong to. When we honor His holy day and His sanctuary with real awe, we're saying yes to being His people.
The covenant hinges on a simple hinge: walking in His statutes, keeping His commandments, doing them. Not just knowing, not just agreeing—doing. Real obedience lives in the feet, not just the head.

Rain in its season, land yielding increase, trees bearing fruit—these aren't abstract promises. They're the farmer's prayer and the gardener's reward. When the land produces like this, even the poorest family eats well.

Threshing flowing into vintage flowing into sowing—the seasons so full of harvest that one blessing spills into the next. You shall eat your bread to the full, dwelling safely on your land. That's the opposite of hunger and fear.

Peace in the land, rest without dread, evil animals removed, no sword passing through. The Lord promises not just provision, but security—a place where families can sleep without terror. That's a parent's dream for their children.

Your enemies fall before you by the sword. Not because you're mighty, but because the Lord Himself stands with you. A few faithful disciples would later learn that the kingdom moves by His power, not theirs.

Five chase a hundred; a hundred chase ten thousand. Sheer impossibility—the math doesn't work unless the Lord is fighting. I've seen the faithful stand against odds that should have crushed them, held up by a strength not their own.

Respect, fruitfulness, multiplication, covenant established—the Lord binds Himself to those who obey. This isn't a trading deal; it's a marriage vow. His respect falls on His people like the sun on a garden.

Store long kept, old pushed out by new—such abundance that you're clearing room for fresh harvest before the old is gone. It speaks of a people whose barns overflow, whose trust in God's provision has been rewarded year after year.

I will set my tent among you. The Tabernacle—God's dwelling pitched in the midst of His people. My soul won't abhor you. After all the failures Israel would know, this promise of presence and non-rejection echoes like a bell we haven't stopped hearing.
I will walk among you. Not watching from heaven, not distant on a throne—walking. The God of the whole earth choosing to stroll through camp, present, available, invested in His people's daily lives.
Out of Egypt, out of slavery, the bars of the yoke broken, heads held upright—redemption work that's already done. The Lord reminds them: you're not saved by works but by grace; now live like it.

But if you will not listen, if you reject, if you break the covenant—the word turns like a door on its hinge. The same God who offers all these mercies will respond to a people who turn away. Love scorned becomes judgment serious.
Rejecting statutes, soul abhorring ordinances, breaking covenant—rebellion isn't passive. It's active turning away from the Lord's command. The soul can choose to hate what the Lord has spoken.

Terror, consumption, fever—disease eats at the eyes and wastes the soul while seed sown vanishes, eaten by enemies. Hopelessness multiplies: your own body fails, your work comes to nothing, your security evaporates.
I will set my face against you—the turning away of favor is worse than any weapon. Your enemies rule; you flee phantom pursuers. When the Lord's face turns, even the air feels hostile.

If you still won't listen after the first wave of correction, I will chastise you sevenfold. The escalation begins: the Lord increases His discipline, hoping each new wave will turn a stubborn heart toward home.
Your sky like iron, your soil like brass—ancient images of a land locked shut. No rain, no mercy, the ground unyielding. It speaks to drought so severe that heaven and earth become a cage.
Strength spent in vain, land yielding nothing, trees bearing no fruit. Work becomes futile; the harvest that seemed certain becomes impossible. A farmer's nightmare made real.
Walking contrary to the Lord, refusing to listen—and the second sevenfold chastisement arrives. Each wave of judgment is meant to say: turn back, turn back, the door is still open.
Wild animals rob children, destroy livestock, reduce the population, leave roads desolate—civilization unravels when the Lord withdraws His hand. The familiar world becomes strange and dangerous.
Still refusing to be reformed, still walking contrary—the heart hardens further. At some point, a people can choose rebellion so completely that even mercy looks like judgment.
I will also walk contrary to you; I will strike you sevenfold for your sins. The third escalation: the Lord's own opposition becomes direct and intensified. He matches their stubbornness with His.
A sword executing covenant vengeance, cities under siege, pestilence spreading, enemies in control—the full weight of war and plague descends. The infrastructure of safety collapses.

Staff of bread broken—the staff being the support, the foundation of life. Ten women baking one loaf in one oven, rationing bread by weight. It's the image of siege and rationing: survival reduced to counting calories.
Still refusing, still walking contrary despite all that has come—the stubbornness is now incurable. The people choose their path even as it leads off a cliff.
I will walk contrary to you in wrath—the Lord's opposition becomes hot, personal, wrathful. Yet even this is judgment with a purpose: to break the will that refuses Him.
Famine so complete that even the unthinkable becomes real. This verse speaks the unspeakable, showing that covenant rebellion leads to the utter collapse of human society and dignity.

High places destroyed, incense altars cut down, idols surrounded by corpses—the false worship they clung to is demolished, and their dead desecrated. Even the religious structures that once felt secure crumble.
Cities laid waste, sanctuaries desolate, offerings unaccepted—the very places meant to connect heaven and earth are rendered hollow. The Lord refuses the fragrance they once imagined pleased Him.
The land itself becomes a wasteland, and enemies who dwell there are astonished at the desolation. It's not just defeat; it's apocalyptic ruination—the land itself mourns.

Scattered among nations, sword drawn out after them, land desolate, cities waste—this is exile, the nightmare that centuries later actually came to pass. Dispersion was the covenant warning written before history.
While they are exiled, the land finally gets its rest—the Sabbath years it never had. Even in judgment, the land is restored and healed. God's justice serves His creation's renewal.

The land rests the years it couldn't while you lived on it—a poignant inversion. The people's refusal to honor Sabbath leads to Sabbath imposed by absence. The land gets what the people wouldn't give.

Faintness in the hearts of those left alive, sound of a driven leaf putting them to flight, fleeing from invisible swords. Terror becomes their constant companion—the opposite of the safety promised at the start.
Stumbling over one another as though fleeing a sword when no one pursues. Panic replaces courage; chaos replaces order. No power to stand before enemies because the courage has been broken.
You will perish among the nations. The land of your enemies will eat you up—dispersed, consumed, absorbed into foreign lands. It's the end of everything Israel was meant to be.
Those left pine away in iniquity, their own and their fathers'—guilt compounds across generations. They're wasting away, not from disease but from the weight of unforgiven rebellion.
If they confess their iniquity and their fathers'—the turning point begins here, so quietly. Repentance starts with naming what was done, owning it fully, refusing to hide behind excuses.
Uncircumcised heart humbled, accepting punishment—confession becomes embodied. They stop fighting the consequences; they submit to what they deserve. That humility opens a door.

I will remember my covenant with Jacob, Isaac, Abraham; I will remember the land. Readers today hear an echo of a God who never forgets His promises, who holds names and covenants even when His people forget Him. Looking back from 2026, how often has the Lord remembered what we've tried to make Him forget?

The land left behind, enjoying Sabbaths while desolate; the people accepting their punishment because they rejected His ordinances. Even their suffering becomes an acknowledgment of the truth they tried to deny.

Yet for all that, when they are in exile, I will not reject them, neither abhor them utterly—the mercy breaks through the judgment. The Lord won't destroy them or break His covenant. Love undercuts judgment.

For their sake I will remember the covenant of their ancestors, whom I brought out of Egypt. The Lord ties His character to His ancient promise: who He is depends on keeping His word to Abraham. Covenant grace holds all the way through.

These are the statutes, ordinances and laws which the Lord made between Him and the children of Israel in Mount Sinai by Moses. A closing seal: this entire chapter of blessing and curse, promise and warning, is the covenant itself, witnessed and recorded.

The Lord begins with a gentle word to Moses: when you want to give yourself to me, I will tell you how. This closing chapter of Leviticus shows that consecration isn't mystery—it's measured, fair, and within reach for any heart that longs to honor Him.

A vow to consecrate a person is serious, yet the Lord offers a way to keep it that doesn't break a poor person. He knows our hearts before we speak; He's already thinking of the widow, the struggling widow who wants to give but has little.

Fifty shekels for a man in his strength—the prime years, when he carries the weight and the hope of his household. The Lord puts a name to the value, not to diminish any soul, but to set a clear boundary so vows don't bankrupt families.

Thirty shekels for a woman—a lower number that speaks to the economics of an ancient household, but notice: she is still valued, still counted, still able to make a vow that the Lord honors. Every voice matters to Him.

Children from five to twenty—the years of learning and growing, when a parent might dedicate a young life to service. The Lord sees their future even when it's unwritten, and His valuation matches what they'll become.

A tiny child, barely remembering words—five shekels for a boy, three for a girl. The Lord doesn't wait for age or understanding; He cherishes the small ones brought to Him in faith, and His measurement is always tender.

At sixty and beyond, the years when strength ebbs but wisdom deepens. Fifteen shekels for an old man, ten for an old woman—the Lord honors the elder still, still counts their prayers, still welcomes their devotion even as the body quiets.

The poorest comes before the priest, and here is mercy written into law: the priest looks not at the scale but at his face, at what he can actually bear. The Lord never meant His altar to be only for the wealthy.

When you give an animal to the Lord, it crosses into a different world—holy now, set apart. There's a solemnity in this: what you hand over is no longer yours to treat as before. The Lord takes it seriously; so must you.

You cannot swap out a good animal for a weaker one, or a weak one for a strong—no bargaining after the vow. This teaches us something about integrity: when we say 'yes' to the Lord, we don't get to renegotiate when circumstances shift.
An unclean animal—one the law says cannot be offered—still has a place before the priest. Even what the law rejects outright, the Lord has a path for. There's always a way for the sincere heart.

The priest's eye is careful, judging not in anger but in fairness—good or bad, each animal gets its true worth named. The Lord teaches us through these laws that judgment can be just, and valuation can be humble.

If he wishes to take his unclean animal back, he adds a fifth to its price—a price for changing his mind, a small tax on backing out. The Lord builds consequences into grace, so we learn the weight of our choices.

A man dedicates his house—not just his livestock, but the very shelter of his family. This is costlier, more personal. The priest evaluates it with care, and what he says stands. The Lord knows this kind of giving cuts deep.

He changes his mind and wants his house back—the Lord allows it, but again, a fifth must be added. There's a pattern: you can undo it, but not without cost. This teaches us that vows aren't chains, yet they aren't cheap.

He dedicates part of his inherited land—a homer of barley brings fifty shekels. Land is memory, livelihood, identity. To give it to the Lord is to say: my future is Yours, my provision is Yours, not my own security.

If the dedication happens in the Jubilee year, the value stands fixed—the great year of release already resets the land's meaning, so the vow stands as spoken. There's an alignment here between God's time and our time.

If he dedicates after the Jubilee, the price drops—fewer years before the land reverts anyway. The Lord's law builds in practicality: the closer to Jubilee, the less you give, because the Lord will return it anyway. He doesn't take what He's already going to restore.
If he wants his land back, the fifth is added again—a redemption tax, the same mercy-and-cost pattern. The Lord always gives you a second thought, but He never lets you think cheap thoughts count.

If he neither redeems it nor keeps the gift—if he tries to pass it to another—that choice locks him out. Once a field is wholly given, it's the Lord's forever. There's a point of no return, and the Lord names it clearly.

In the Jubilee it becomes holy and belongs to the priests—the servants of the altar. The land that was once his now feeds those who feed the people spiritually. One man's devotion becomes another man's provision.

A man dedicates land he bought, not inherited—land without family memory or claim. Even a purchased field, stripped of heritage, can be made holy. The Lord receives what we freely choose to give, not only what binds us by blood.

The priest counts the years until Jubilee and names a price reflecting that span. The Lord's law is mathematically just: time matters, and what you lose in years shapes what you owe. Nothing escapes His accounting.

In the Jubilee, the field returns to him from whom it was bought—the original owner, the true possessor. Even if a man gave it away, even if he meant it to be forever gone, the Jubilee restores what was lost. The Lord never lets a sale be truly final.

All valuations follow the sanctuary shekel—the official measure, unchanging, universal. The Lord's measure is not like the world's, which shifts with hunger and greed. His standard holds steady for every person and every gift.

No one may dedicate the firstborn—it's already the Lord's by the law itself. Some things are not ours to vow, because they already belong to Him. This teaches us wisdom: to recognize what's beyond our power to give.

If it's an unclean animal—a donkey, a camel—he buys it back with a fifth added, or it's sold. The firstborn is the Lord's, but if it cannot be offered, there's still a way to release it. Even in law, the Lord leaves room to breathe.

A devoted thing—fully devoted—can never be redeemed or sold; it remains most holy. This is the highest vow, the ultimate gift: no backing out, no buyback, only holiness. Some surrenders are meant to be forever.

A person devoted to the Lord cannot be ransomed—an ancient rule reflecting the gravity of a life wholly given. Whether this speaks of temple service or a deeper consequence, the point stands: total devotion has no middle ground.

All the tithe belongs to the Lord—a tenth of seed and fruit, set aside before anything else is claimed. The farmer looks at his harvest and says: You first. This is the rhythm of gratitude, written into the soil itself.

If he redeems his tithe—takes it back in silver—a fifth is added to its worth. Even the tenth, which is already the Lord's, costs something to reclaim. The Lord doesn't begrudge us, but He never lets us imagine provision is free.

The tithe of herds or flocks: every tenth animal that passes under the rod belongs to the Lord. No picking the strongest, no choosing favorites—the rod chooses, and the Lord takes what comes. He wants what you cannot control, so you learn to trust.

Don't search or judge whether it's good or bad—don't look to save a weak one. Accept the tenth that falls; both it and any swap are equally holy. The Lord asks for surrender, not strategy; for trust, not cleverness.

Readers today hear an echo in this final verse: these laws, given at Sinai so long ago, still teach us that the Lord is generous—He takes our gifts seriously, offers buyback grace, and never forgets the poor. As of 2026-10, His care hasn't changed.
